title: Alum Rock Union Elementary School District General Obligation Bond
summary: Measure P authorizes Alum Rock Union Elementary School District to issue $100 million in general obligation bonds, under Proposition 39, to repair leaky roofs and plumbing, replace HVAC systems, and upgrade emergency communication and security systems districtwide. It requires 55% voter approval and is projected to hold the average tax rate below $26 per $100,000 of assessed value, raising an estimated $6.3 million a year while bonds are outstanding. The district's other November 2026 measure, Measure O, is a separate $310 flat parcel tax requiring two-thirds approval; Measure P is a distinct, ad valorem bond mechanism with its own 55% threshold.
what_it_really_means: The 75-word ballot question voters will mark reads: 'With funds that cannot be taken by the State or Federal government, shall Alum Rock Union Elementary School District's measure to repair leaky roofs and plumbing; replace heating, ventilation, and air conditioning; and upgrade emergency communication and security systems be adopted, authorizing $100 million of bonds with legal rates, without increasing current tax rates, average levies below $26 per $100,000 of assessed valuation (raising $6.3 million annually while outstanding), audits, independent oversight, and disclosure of all spending?' This is Resolution No. 02-26/27, considered at the same July 16, 2026 board meeting as the parcel tax resolution behind Measure O. Per the district's own board-meeting item summary, the resolution presents 'a $100 million bond measure to District voters under Prop. 39 (55% vote)' financing projects on a 'specific Project List attached as Appendix A,' with Appendix B as the 75-word ballot label and Appendix C as the Tax Rate Statement. Calling the election required a two-thirds vote of the five-member Board of Trustees (four 'aye' votes), the same threshold Measure O's companion resolution needed.

The phrase 'without increasing current tax rates' is doing real work: the district's own Measure P information flyer states plainly that 'Measure P extends but does not increase the current tax rate.' Alum Rock voters already pay property tax to retire four prior facility bonds, Measure G (2008), Measure J (2012), Measure I (2016), and Measure S (2022), all passed under the same Proposition 39, 55%-threshold framework. Measure P is not layered as a brand-new levy on top of an otherwise-untaxed base; it is calibrated to keep the combined tax rate roughly where it already sits as older bond series retire, an approach standard among California school districts that run sequential bond programs. Because the district's official Tax Rate Statement (Appendix C) could not be read for this analysis (see below), the precise mechanics of how the rate is held flat, and the exact peak-year rate and final payoff year, are the district's own estimate and were not independently verified here.

Unlike the district's companion Measure M-style bond comparisons in neighboring districts, no source reached for this analysis disclosed ARUSD's total projected debt service (principal plus interest) for Measure P. The Registrar's Impartial Analysis and the Primary Argument In-Favor, both of which would typically carry or reference that figure, returned only generic Cloudflare-protection HTML rather than readable PDF content when fetched directly; the district's board-book PDF for the July 16, 2026 meeting included only the one-page staff summary of Resolution No. 02-26/27, not the attached Appendix C Tax Rate Statement itself. Taking the ballot label's own disclosed figure, roughly $6.3 million raised annually 'while outstanding,' as a rough guide: if that annual levy runs for something on the order of 25 to 30 years, consistent with the multi-decade repayment periods typical of Proposition 39 school bonds elsewhere in the county, cumulative debt service would land in a broad range of roughly $160 million to $190 million, meaning total repayment of somewhere around 1.6 to 1.9 times the $100 million borrowed. This is this analysis's own back-of-envelope inference from the disclosed annual figure, not a number stated in any source reached; voters relying on the district's own Tax Rate Statement for the actual peak rate, final fiscal year, and total debt service should look for Appendix C directly, which was not accessible here.

Measure P requires an independent Citizens' Bond Oversight Committee (CBOC) under Proposition 39 (Education Code Section 15278 et seq.), and the district's own bond web page confirms it already operates one: an 'Independent Citizen's Bond Oversight Committee' that the district describes as overseeing bond Measures G, J, I, and S, with seven volunteer seats (a business-community representative, a senior-citizens'-organization representative, a taxpayer-association representative, two at-large community members, a parent of an enrolled student, and a parent active in a parent organization). The district's page frames the CBOC as a standing body rather than a series of separate one-bond committees, so Measure P most plausibly extends the existing committee's scope to a fifth bond series rather than creating a wholly new oversight structure, though no source reached explicitly confirmed the committee has formally been asked to take on Measure P oversight as of this writing. This CBOC requirement is entirely separate from, and does not overlap with, Measure O: because Measure O is a parcel tax rather than a Proposition 39 bond, it carries no CBOC requirement at all, only the lighter statutory annual spending report under Government Code Section 50075.1. A voter approving both measures is authorizing two different accountability regimes: a mandatory, seven-member independent audit-and-oversight committee for the bond (Measure P), and a district-filed annual report with no outside committee for the parcel tax (Measure O).

The district's Measure P project list, published in its own frequently-asked-questions flyer, is considerably broader than the ballot label's three headline categories (roofs/plumbing, HVAC, emergency communication/security). It separately lists: updating kitchens and replacing outdated equipment; reconfiguring student drop-off and pick-up areas; installing additional drinking fountains and hydration stations; replacing aging portable classrooms; repairing playgrounds, playfields, sidewalks, and parking lots; installing fencing, security cameras, and alarms; providing indoor facilities for physical education and student activities; modernizing outdated electrical, communication, and network infrastructure; and modernizing and restoring aging restrooms and sewer lines. None of these categories carries a dollar figure or a per-school allocation in any source reached, so, as with comparable Proposition 39 bonds elsewhere in the county, the Board of Trustees retains discretion over which of these projects are actually funded, in what order, and at which campuses; the full legal 'Bond Project List' text (Appendix A to Resolution No. 02-26/27), which would normally spell out any priority disclaimers or per-campus detail, was not accessible in this research.

A benefit not stated anywhere in the 75-word ballot label: the district's own flyer states that 'voter approval of Measure P will allow the district to qualify for State matching funds' under the state's School Facility Program. This is standard for Proposition 39 local bonds, which typically serve as the required local match for state facilities grants, but a voter reading only the ballot question would not know that a yes vote also unlocks eligibility for additional money from Sacramento.

The district's Measure P web page also lists a 'Community Benefit Agreement' among its 'Related Resources,' consisting of a Project Labor Agreement dated 2016 and a first amendment to it. A Project Labor Agreement typically binds contractors on covered construction work to specific labor terms (such as using hiring halls and following agreed wage and apprenticeship provisions) before they can bid. This document predates Measure P by a decade and was not confirmed in this research to apply specifically to Measure P-funded projects rather than to the district's construction program generally, but its placement under the Measure P information page signals it is treated as applicable to bond-funded construction going forward, something not evident from the ballot title.

If a household owns property in Alum Rock Union Elementary School District, the November 2026 ballot asks for two separate, differently-structured tax commitments from the same district in the same election: Measure O's flat $310 per parcel (regardless of assessed value) and Measure P's ad valorem rate of up to roughly $26 per $100,000 of assessed value. For illustration only, since no source reached published a combined per-household total, a property assessed at $400,000 would pay approximately $310 (Measure O) plus roughly $104 (Measure P, at $26 per $100,000) for a combined roughly $414 per year if both measures pass; a property assessed at $800,000 would pay the same flat $310 plus roughly $208, for a combined roughly $518 per year. These are this analysis's own arithmetic from the two measures' disclosed rates, not a figure either measure's own materials publish jointly.

fiscal_impact.state_cost: none directly. The measure does not obligate state funds, though the district states that voter approval will help it qualify for state School Facility Program matching grants, a separate, discretionary state appropriation not guaranteed by this measure.
fiscal_impact.local_cost: Alum Rock Union Elementary School District property owners pay via an ad valorem property tax levy. The ballot question and the district's own Measure P flyer estimate an average annual tax rate below $26 per $100,000 of assessed valuation, raising approximately $6.3 million annually while bonds are outstanding, without increasing the district's current combined tax rate. The official Tax Rate Statement (Appendix C to Resolution No. 02-26/27), which would state the peak-year rate, the final fiscal year of collection, and total debt service, was not accessible in this research.
fiscal_impact.revenue_change: Increases the district's bond-fund revenue by an estimated $6.3 million annually while the bonds authorized by this measure are outstanding, funded by property tax, not the district's general fund or a parcel tax.
fiscal_impact.ongoing_vs_one_time: The $100 million bond authorization is issued in series over time as the district needs project funds, not all at once. Repayment is a recurring annual property tax obligation for a period the district's Tax Rate Statement would specify exactly; that figure was not accessible in this research, but Proposition 39 school bonds of this size typically run 25 to 30-plus years.
fiscal_impact.narrative: The headline figures, $100 million in bonds and an average rate below $26 per $100,000, describe the borrowing authorization and the average annual cost, not the total repayment cost. Because the total debt service (principal plus interest) was not disclosed in any source reached, voters cannot see from the ballot question or this analysis exactly how much more than $100 million will ultimately be repaid; based on the disclosed $6.3 million annual figure and typical multi-decade terms for this bond type, total repayment plausibly falls somewhere between roughly $160 million and $190 million, but that range is this analysis's own estimate, not an official figure. The measure is also explicitly framed by the district as holding the tax rate flat rather than raising it, because it is timed to follow the district's four prior facility bonds (Measures G, J, I, S) as they retire; a voter comparing only 'before Measure P' and 'after Measure P' tax bills should understand that a same-district tax obligation for facilities bonds already exists and this measure aims to continue rather than add to it, though the near-term year-by-year mechanics of that transition were not confirmed here.

new_taxes: An ad valorem property tax levy on all taxable property within Alum Rock Union Elementary School District, imposed to repay up to $100,000,000 in general obligation bonds authorized under Proposition 39 (55% voter approval). The district estimates an average annual rate below $26 per $100,000 of assessed valuation, raising approximately $6.3 million annually while bonds are outstanding, timed to avoid increasing the district's current combined tax rate as prior bond series (Measures G, J, I, and S) retire.

new_spending_areas: Repairing and replacing leaky roofs and plumbing systems districtwide.
Replacing inefficient heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning (HVAC) systems.
Upgrading fire alarms, emergency communication systems, and security systems including fencing, cameras, and alarms.
Updating kitchens, replacing outdated equipment, reconfiguring student drop-off and pick-up areas, and installing additional drinking fountains and hydration stations.
Replacing aging portable classrooms; repairing playgrounds, playfields, sidewalks, and parking lots.

Providing indoor facilities for physical education and student activities; modernizing outdated electrical, communication, and network infrastructure; modernizing and restoring aging restrooms and replacing leaky plumbing systems, aging sewer lines, and pipes.
spending.funding_source: General obligation bonds secured by an ad valorem property tax on real property within Alum Rock Union Elementary School District, issued in series over time up to the $100,000,000 authorized principal amount, requiring 55% voter approval under Proposition 39 (2000).

control_and_power: The Alum Rock Union Elementary School District Board of Trustees adopted Resolution No. 02-26/27 at its July 16, 2026 meeting, placing Measure P on the ballot; per the board's own meeting materials, calling the election required a two-thirds vote of the five-member Board (four 'aye' votes), the same threshold used for the companion Measure O parcel-tax resolution considered at the same meeting. Once approved by voters, the Board of Trustees decides which projects on the Bond Project List are funded, in what order, and at which campuses; no source reached for this analysis disclosed a per-project or per-campus dollar allocation. State law (Education Code Section 15278 et seq.) requires the district to maintain an independent Citizens' Bond Oversight Committee, and the district's own bond web page describes a standing seven-member CBOC that already oversees the district's four prior facility bonds (Measures G, J, I, and S); that committee most plausibly extends to Measure P as a fifth bond series, though no source reached confirmed this formally. The CBOC's statutory role is to confirm bond proceeds are spent on listed facilities projects rather than salaries, pensions, or benefits, and to review independent annual audits; it does not set project priorities or approve individual expenditures in advance, a decision that remains with the Board. This oversight structure is entirely separate from Measure O's accountability mechanism (a statutory annual spending report with no outside committee), since Measure O is a parcel tax rather than a Proposition 39 bond.
loopholes: The Bond Project List spans a wide range of categories (roofs, plumbing, HVAC, kitchens, drop-off areas, drinking fountains, portables, playgrounds, sidewalks, parking lots, fencing, security systems, indoor PE facilities, electrical/network infrastructure, restrooms, and sewer lines) with no dollar figure attached to any individual project or campus in any source reached, meaning the Board of Trustees, not voters, decides after the election which specific projects are funded and in what sequence.

The measure's official Tax Rate Statement (Appendix C to Resolution No. 02-26/27), which would disclose the peak-year tax rate, the final fiscal year of collection, and total debt service including interest, could not be read for this analysis: the Registrar's Impartial Analysis and Primary Argument In-Favor PDFs returned only Cloudflare-protection HTML rather than their actual content, and the district's own board-book PDF included only the one-page staff summary of the resolution, not its attached appendices. Voters approving the measure are relying on figures (the below-$26-per-$100,000 average rate, the $6.3 million annual raise) that are the district's own estimates and, per standard Proposition 39 bond language seen in comparable districts, are typically non-binding and subject to change based on the timing of bond sales and future assessed valuation, though ARUSD's own disclaimer language could not be independently confirmed here.

The Citizens' Bond Oversight Committee required for this bond confirms spending complies with the project-list categories and reviews audit results, but (consistent with how Proposition 39 CBOCs generally operate) has no authority to set spending priorities, approve individual expenditures before they are made, or reallocate funds between projects; that decision-making stays with the Board of Trustees.

No opposing argument was filed with the Registrar of Voters for Measure P, so the official ballot pamphlet will contain only the case in favor, even though the Silicon Valley Taxpayers Association has publicly recommended a NO vote.
unexpected_provisions: Voter approval of Measure P is stated by the district to make it eligible to 'qualify for State matching funds' under the state's School Facility Program, an additional funding consequence not mentioned in the 75-word ballot question itself.

The district's own Measure P information page lists a 2016 Project Labor Agreement and its amendment among the measure's 'Related Resources,' suggesting bond-funded construction work will be governed by pre-existing labor terms (such as hiring-hall and wage provisions for contractors) that predate this specific bond and are not disclosed anywhere in the ballot label.

The same November 3, 2026 ballot carries a second, unrelated Alum Rock Union Elementary School District measure, Measure O, a $310 flat-per-parcel education tax requiring two-thirds approval (versus Measure P's 55% threshold) and funded through a general-fund parcel levy rather than property-tax-secured borrowing; voters should not assume the two measures share a mechanism, rate structure, or accountability regime simply because they appear on the same district's ballot in the same election.

Measure P is explicitly designed to avoid increasing the district's current combined tax rate by timing its levy against the retirement of four prior facility bonds (Measures G, J, I, and S); a voter unaware of that context might assume 'without increasing current tax rates' means no facilities-bond tax currently exists, when in fact Alum Rock property owners have been paying one continuously since at least 2008.
pros: The measure funds facility needs, leaky roofs, plumbing, HVAC, and emergency communication and security systems, that directly affect student and staff safety and are the kind of deferred maintenance many older school buildings accumulate.

The district states the measure extends rather than increases the current tax rate, timed against the retirement of prior bond series, so it is not presented as a net-new burden on top of what property owners already pay for school facilities.

The measure carries the accountability structure required of all Proposition 39 school bonds: independent annual audits, a Citizens' Bond Oversight Committee, and a stated prohibition on using proceeds for administrator salaries, pensions, or benefits.

Voter approval is stated to help the district qualify for additional state School Facility Program matching funds, potentially extending the reach of the $100 million beyond what local taxpayers alone provide.

The district has passed four prior facility bonds (2008, 2012, 2016, 2022), each exceeding the 55% threshold by a wide margin (71% to 79% approval), which supporters could point to as a track record of voter confidence and administration of bond funds.

No opposing argument was filed with the Registrar of Voters, indicating limited organized local opposition to the specific measure text, even though some organizations oppose it on general tax-policy grounds.
cons: The measure's own official Tax Rate Statement, which would disclose the true total cost of borrowing (principal plus interest) and the final year of repayment, was not accessible in this research; based only on the disclosed $6.3 million annual figure, total repayment plausibly runs to roughly 1.6 to 1.9 times the $100 million borrowed, a cost not stated in the ballot question.

The Bond Project List spans many categories with no dollar figure assigned to any individual project or campus in any source reached, so voters are authorizing a large sum without knowing which specific projects will be built, at which schools, or in what order.

The Silicon Valley Taxpayers Association recommends a NO vote, listing Measure P among the local tax and bond measures it opposes and citing the cumulative burden of local tax measures, including this district's own companion Measure O parcel tax, on the same countywide ballot.

Alum Rock voters are being asked to approve two separate tax mechanisms from the same district in the same election, Measure O's flat per-parcel tax and Measure P's ad valorem bond levy, which together impose a larger combined annual cost on property owners than either measure disclosed alone.

Neither the Registrar's Impartial Analysis nor the Primary Argument In-Favor could be read in full for this research because both returned inaccessible, Cloudflare-protected content rather than readable PDF text, so voters relying on typical online research tools may find those documents similarly hard to access.

The district has had recent governance turnover, including a new superintendent hired on a three-year contract around the same summer the board finalized both the parcel tax and bond resolutions, which is relevant context for voters assessing the district's administrative capacity even though no source ties it directly to Measure P's spending plan.
